title: Staged cache-aware decoder orchestration — proposal
content:
Goal
---
Sketch a lightweight, implementable orchestration layer that: (1) consciously stages prefill/decoder work with cache-awareness; (2) enforces stream priorities across heterogeneous GPUs while keeping single-request latency SLOs; (3) supports micro-slicing of decode work to improve head-of-line fairness; and (4) exposes tuning knobs for batching and kernel selection. This is a collaboration/starting point for runtime + infra + perf teams to agree on experiments and a minimal viable control loop.

Motivation / observed pain points
-------------------------------
- Heavy prefill bursts (long contexts) clog KV cache warm paths and cause downstream decoder stalls for short, high-priority streams.
- Current handshake model treats prefill and decode as independent phases; that creates head-of-line blocking when prefill I/O and KV reconstruction overlap with low-latency decode tasks.
- Static microbatch sizes and blind batching lead to poor p95 for interactive tiers even when average throughput is good.
- Kernel selection is currently per-model+device but not aware of real-time sequence-length mix; switching kernels mid-request is possible but not coordinated with scheduling.
- We need a middle ground between full pipeline overlap (complex) and strict separation (wasteful) — hence "staged" orchestration.

Key concepts and definitions
---------------------------
- Stage: a logical unit of work in the request lifecycle. For our purposes: input-ingest, prefill (KV reconstruction + attention warm-up), decode-slices (one or more short decode micro-steps), emit/stream.
- Micro-slice: a small decode unit (e.g., 8–32 tokens) scheduled atomically on a decode lane to reduce blocking and improve interleaving across streams.
- Decode lane: a runtime worker/queue bound to a specific device and kernel profile. Each lane has properties: device-type, kernel-profile, latency-SLO, priority-buckets.
- Cache window: time after a prefill when KV cache is considered "hot" for that model/seqlen fingerprint. We track per-model per-worker windows to enable aggressive reuse.
- Priority buckets: metadata attached to requests (interactive, background-batch, reserved-dedicated).

High-level design
-----------------
1) Staged admission controller (lightweight policy):
   - On request arrival, perform cheap classification: expected prefill cost (ctx_len), decode estimate (expected tokens), priority.
   - If prefill cost >> threshold and priority is low, admit into background prefill queue; otherwise, attempt fast-path.

2) Prefill staging with cache-awareness:
   - Prefills can be executed in either "eager warm" (fill KV on-device ahead of decode) or "lazy fill" (inject KV fragments into cache on-demand during first micro-slices).
   - Decision heuristic: if expected decode tokens < micro-slice threshold and device has other high-priority lanes, choose lazy fill; else choose eager.
   - Track a compact per-worker fingerprint store: model-id + ctx-window hash -> last-warmed-timestamp (small LRU). This allows us to skip full prefill when warm.

3) Micro-sliced decode with cooperative prefill overlap:
   - Decode work is split into micro-slices. The scheduler interleaves micro-slices from multiple streams based on priority and cache-warmth.
   - If a decode micro-slice lacks KV entries, the runtime can opportunistically pull a single KV fragment (mini-prefill) and resume next slice to avoid long blocking.

4) Lane-aware kernel switching policy:
   - Each decode lane advertises supported kernels and the switching cost (ms) between kernels on that device for specific sequence-length regimes.
   - When scheduling a micro-slice, prefer running it on a lane with an already-active kernel that matches the slice's seqlen; amortize kernel switch costs across bursts.

5) Backpressure and pacing: 
   - If prefill queues grow beyond dynamic threshold (derived from target p99 latency and available warm windows), throttle low-priority prefill admission.
   - Implement soft pacing tokens for interactive streams: allow up to N micro-slices queued per-request; beyond that, buffer in request-side backpressure until previous slices are emitted or timeout triggers graceful fallback to smaller model.

Priority handling and fairness
-----------------------------
- Maintain separate lane queues for priority buckets but permit limited interleaving: high-priority streams get preemptive micro-slice slots (m per second) on all lanes for short bursts.
- Use token-budget accounting across the lifetime of a request: allocate a micro-slice budget per priority and enforce through the admission controller. This prevents abusive long contexts from throttling interactive lanes.

KV cache lifecycle and eviction hints
------------------------------------
- Instead of global LRU eviction, use multi-grain hints: (a) hot fingerprint TTL; (b) per-customer reuse score; (c) lane-affinity hint for recently used model-kernel combos.
- Eviction is cooperative: when a lane needs memory, it emits a "suggested-evict" list (fingerprints) and the central GC process reconciles across workers to avoid thrashing.

Failure modes and fallbacks
---------------------------
- If a lane experiences heavy kernel-switch thrashing, fall back to "isolate" mode: pin high-priority streams to a dedicated kernel lane and migrate low-priority workloads elsewhere.
- If cache warm-hit fails during micro-slice and latency SLO is at risk, trigger graceful fallback to shorter model variant or emit partial streaming result with a downstream re-ask.

Performance targets and success metrics
-------------------------------------
- Target: reduce interactive p95 by 20% under mixed workload (25% long prefill-heavy, 60% short interactive, 15% background) compared to baseline.
- Maintain overall throughput within 5% of baseline for same GPU footprint.
- Measure: p50/p95/p99 latency per priority, kernel-switch frequency per-lane, cache warm-hit ratio, fraction of micro-slices preempted.

Implementation plan (phased)
---------------------------
Phase 0 — experiments (2–3 sprints):
  - Instrument fingerprints and simple per-worker warm-window store.
  - Implement micro-slices in the decode execution path (configurable slice size).
  - Add lightweight admission classifier and background prefill queue.

Phase 1 — lane primitives & policies (3–4 sprints):
  - Lane metadata, priority queues, kernel-switch cost tracking.
  - KV eviction hints and cooperative GC prototype.
  - Basic pacing tokens for interactive buckets.

Phase 2 — policy tuning + observability (2 sprints):
  - Automatic knob tuning, dashboards for kernel switches, warm-hit heatmaps, p95 by priority.
  - Shadow traffic experiments against canary fleets.

Phase 3 — rollout and refinements (2–3 sprints):
  - Canary -> gradual rollout to hosted API, monitor fallbacks and throughput.
  - Add model-variant automatic fallback logic and per-customer SLAs.

Open questions / tradeoffs
------------------------
- Micro-slice size vs kernel efficiency: tiny slices help latency fairness but can drastically reduce kernel throughput. Need microbenchmarks across our common kernels (FP16/4-bit) and seqlen distributions.
- How much state is acceptable in per-worker fingerprint store? Memory vs hit rate tradeoff.
- Should we centralize eviction decisions or keep them local with periodic reconciliation? Centralization gives global view but adds coordination latency.
- Interaction with Dedicated customers who expect capacity isolation — we must ensure reserved lanes and different priority semantics.

Benchmarks to run
-----------------
- Synthetic mix: 60% short (<=64 tokens), 25% long (>=2048 prefill), 15% batch; measure p95/p99.
- Kernel switch amortization test: issue variable-length sequences and instrument time lost to switching.
- Cache warm-hit model: preload warm windows and measure fraction of prefill-skips and their downstream impact.

Next steps / action items
------------------------
- Jordan: prototype micro-slicing abstraction in the decode worker (due 2025-01-29).
- Marco: implement compact fingerprint LRU and expose warm-window API (due 2025-02-05).
- Sam: draft telemetry dashboard (kernel switches, warm-hits, p95 by priority) and a Linear board for experiments (due 2025-02-09).
- Sync: schedule cross-team design review with infra/serving/console for observability and rollout plan (target 2025-02-12).

Appendix: example admission heuristic (pseudocode)
------------------------------------------------
- compute cost = ctx_len * prefill_cost_factor + est_decode_tokens * decode_cost_factor
- if priority == interactive and ctx_len <= eager_threshold => fast-path (eager prefill)
- else if priority == background => schedule background prefill
- else if worker.fingerprint_hot(model, ctx_hash) => fast-path lazy-prefill + micro-slice immediate
- else => if worker.util < util_threshold => eager prefill else lazy-prefill

Notes / rationale: keep the admission heuristic cheap — avoid clusters of RPCs during admit. When in doubt, prefer decisions that keep short interactive latency low even at small throughput cost.

This doc is intentionally high-level: the goal is to converge quickly on a handful of experiments that will answer the kernel-switch and micro-slice efficiency questions. Please annotate with concerns or data pointers before the design review.
